message.content:
Short answer: **it's safe only if you're the sole person working on that branch** — and even then, you have to push it correctly. Rebasing rewrites history, so the commits on the remote and the commits in your local repo stop being the same objects.

## The rule

Never rebase commits that someone else may have built on. Pushing alone doesn't make it dangerous — *other people pulling* does.

## Safe cases

- Your personal feature branch (`alice/login-fix`), nobody else has checked it out or based work on it, not merged anywhere.
- `git pull --rebase` to sync your branch with `main`: this replays **your new local commits** on top of the remote tip. It doesn't rewrite anything already published. This is fine and is the right way to stay current.
- A PR that's still yours and untouched, ideally rebased right before merging to keep the window small.

## Unsafe cases

- Shared/long-lived branches: `main`, `develop`, a team branch, a release branch.
- Anyone has opened a PR against it, or based a branch on it.
- A reviewer is mid-review — force-pushing detaches their inline comments from the commits they anchor to.
- Commits have already been merged into another branch. Rebasing then creates duplicate-but-different commits and painful tangles.
- Stacked PRs / Gerrit / a branch another teammate's work sits on top of.
- Branch is protected and blocks force-push (that's a signal, not an obstacle to work around).

## How to do it when it *is* your branch

```bash
git rebase main                 # or: git rebase --onto main <old-base> my-branch

# push the rewritten history — never bare --force
git push --force-with-lease origin my-branch
```

`--force-with-lease` aborts if someone pushed to the branch while you were rebasing, which is exactly the "you thought you were alone but you weren't" case. Bare `git push --force` silently deletes their work.

Then:
- Tell your team in the PR — one sentence, *"rebased on main, history rewritten."*
- Anyone with the old branch needs `git fetch` and then `git reset --hard origin/my-branch` (if they have no local work of their own on it), or `git rebase origin/my-branch` on top of their new commits. A plain `git pull` will create a tangled merge commit.

## "I already broke it"

Your work isn't lost. Rebase saves the old tip:

```bash
git reflog                    # find the pre-rebase commit, e.g. abc1234 HEAD@{2}
git reset --hard abc1234      # or: git push --force-with-lease origin abc1234:my-branch
```

## "Am I alone on this branch?" — check before you rebase

```bash
git log --format='%an' origin/my-branch ^main | sort -u   # who authored the commits
git log --branches --remotes --contains origin/my-branch   # is anything else built on the tip?
```

## If you're unsure, don't rebase

Merge `main` into your branch instead. You get an extra merge commit and slightly noisier history — that's the entire cost. The alternative, rewriting published history a teammate depends on, costs their afternoon. Most teams settle this by rebasing/squashing only at merge time via the PR's "squash and merge," which never touches shared history.
message.reasoning:
The user asks a general Git question: "Is it safe to rebase a branch I've already pushed?" This is a conceptual question, not a creative task. Should I load a skill? The skills available are about brainstorming, debugging, etc. None matches a straightforward Q&A about git rebase safety. So answer directly.

Let me give a thorough, accurate answer.

Key points:
- Rebasing rewrites commit history → new commit SHAs. Anyone who has the old commits will diverge.
- Safe if: you're the only one on the branch (personal feature branch), or branch not yet merged, and you communicate.
- Unsafe if: others have based work on it, shared/long-lived branch (main, develop), protected branch, or a PR is under review with people reviewing specific commits.
- Alternatives: merge instead of rebase; use `git merge` or rebase only your own local commits with `git rebase --onto`, or use squash-merge at PR time.
- If you must rebase a pushed branch: `git push --force-with-lease` (never plain `--force`), tell collaborators, do it right before merging to minimize window.
- Recovery: `git reflog`, ORIG_HEAD.
- Special cases: `git pull --rebase` on your own branch is fine generally (it replays your local commits onto remote's tip; but if remote branch has commits you authored and someone else pulled... careful). Actually `git pull --rebase` rebases your local commits on top of remote-tracking branch. That's the recommended way to sync without creating merge commits, and it doesn't rewrite already-pushed commits — it rewrites your new local ones. Good.
- If you rebase a branch that has been merged into another branch, you'll cause problems.
- Gerrit / stacked PR considerations.
- Force-push triggers new CI runs, closes/updates PRs.
- Note: a rebase where nothing changes (e.g., rebase onto the same base with fast-forward) may be a no-op.
- GitHub: if the PR was opened from the branch, force-push updates the PR, keeps discussion but loses per-commit review anchors; GitHub stores the old commits in the PR timeline though (they remain accessible via the force-push event). But reviewers' comment positions can be lost.
- Rule of thumb: "Never rebase commits that others may have built on."
- Also mention: rebasing your local main onto origin/main is fine if you haven't pushed.
- Safe-ish practice: don't rebase after others pulled; prefer `git rerere`? Not needed.

Also mention checking who's on the branch: `git log --format='%an' origin/branch | sort -u`, or check for other refs pointing to those commits: `git log --branches --remotes --contains <old-tip>`.

Also mention protected branches on GitHub/GitLab that block force-push.

Length: medium. Provide a decision checklist.
